newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fuji TV debut draws investors, boosts Nikkei.
newsitem.headline: Fuji TV debut draws investors, boosts Nikkei.

text.p: Investors tired of pricey blue chips and worried by a stalling stock market flocked to buy shares in highly-touted broadcaster Fuji Television Network Inc when it debuted on the Tokyo bourse on Friday.

The interest propelled the shares to a high of 700,000 yen ($5,932) at one point in the morning session. They closed at 660,000 yen ($5,593) after adding 7,000 yen to their opening price and a premium of 110,000 yen to the initial offer price.
"The first trade was done at a satisfactory level," Fuji TV president Hisashi Hieda told reporters after the market closed.
The successful listing eased one of the many anxieties hanging over the stock market and helped the Nikkei 225 average to a higher close of 19,604.46, up 128.61 points.
Of the 113 billion yen ($957 million) Fuji TV obtained from the listing, Hieda said 90 billion yen ($762 million) would be used to repay loans and the remainder to produce software.
"We must also think of share splits and dividend increases for our shareholders," he added.

The president of what is the third Japanese broadcaster to go public said earlier that the firm expects a parent current profit of 22.70 billion yen ($192 million) in the year to the end of March 1998, down from 26.64 billion yen ($225 million) the previous year, due to costs resulting from moving its headquarters.
In the days leading to the listing, brokers had kept fingers crossed for a successful start and the smooth debut had them sighing with relief.
Many had feared a failure would worsen market sentiment and prospects for another big launch, Central Japan Railways Co, which is expected in October.

"From the performance of Fuji TV and the stock market today it seems that the supply/demand situation is not bad as people think, even with Nomura on the sidelines," said Haruo Nakaharu, a director at Toyo Securities.

Concerns about the listing had grown after Fuji TV's lead manager Yamaichi Securities Co Ltdwas raided recently on suspicion of having done illegal stock deals with a corporate racketeer. This led to worries that Yamaichi might not be able to advertise the new issue aggressively.
To add to the concerns, Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd, is currently out of the market, undergoing punishment for illicit deals with the same racketeer.
Some market sources said the slow state of the bourse was a blessing in disguise for Fuji TV.
"Since there were few issues attractive to buyers, investors concentrated on Fuji TV's shares," said Hiroyuki Nakai, chief investment strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
Fuji TV is known for innovative programming that includes many comedy shows which are popular with teenage viewers.

Earlier this year it said it would join media tycoon Rupert Murdoch's digital satellite broadcasting venture Japan Sky Broadcasting Co. Brokers said that although it remained to be seen how successful the business would be, it provided investors with a future to speculate about.
"It's slim pickings in the entertainment sector and Fuji TV is good for investors who want balance in their portfolios," said Richard May, research analyst at D.E. Shaw Securities Japan.

"Japanese private investors who know the brand name will be buying and hiking up the prices in the beginning," he said. "At least a month is needed before the share prices normalise and long-term investors start to buy." ($1=118 yen)
